newsitem.title: USA: Pre-Greenspan jitters may push U.S. bond mkt lower.
newsitem.headline: Pre-Greenspan jitters may push U.S. bond mkt lower.

text.p: The desire to avoid long or short positions in what some feel is an overvalued market may push U.S. Treasuries prices lower before next week's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony, bond market players said on Friday.

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan testifies before Congress next Wednesday and Thursday and few players seemed to have the stomach to establish long or short positions before hearing what he will say on the U.S. economy.

"Money managers are bound to edge out of the long end (of the bond market) and stocks toward cash on Monday and Tuesday," said David Munro, chief U.S. economist at High Frequency Economics. He warned investors are bound to make something bearish for stocks and bonds out of the central bank chief's testimony.

"What else but hawkish Fedspeak can be expected from a conservative Fed chairman looking at tight labor markets, indications of scattered wage heating and what he has dubbed as 'one-time' dampers on benefits gains," Munro said.

"We have some supply coming up, but no new meaningful economic news before he speaks which is why we may see a downtick," said Thomas Pearl, a government trader at Chase Securities Inc. The U.S. Treasury auctions three- and six-month bills on Monday and two- and five-year notes on Tuesday and Wednesday, respectively.
"People are afraid he might say something negative and with the market up at the high level it is, we may see a bit of a downtrade," Pearl said.
Matt Alexy, chief market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston, noted that Greenspan has held the same views for quite a while, making investors curious to see if he has anything different to say.
In a market many see as overvalued, Alexy said, "A lot of investors are trying to get to neutral going into his testimony. That's what a lot of the selloff seen in the last few days was all about."
Bond prices were somewhat improved around midday Friday after seeing large losses on Thursday and some erosion on Wednesday despite the release of weak inflationary data.
However, a money manager at a major firm said the market was getting ahead of itself in worrying about what Greenspan might say.
"He hasn't said anything in a long time. I wouldn't worry about it," the manager said.
